claims.text: Slightly increasing phosphorus concentration will improve the alloy's glass-forming ability.
Slightly increasing phosphorus concentration will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The baseline phosphorus-containing alloy forms an amorphous phase upon rapid quenching.
The proposed intervention is a modest increase in phosphorus content relative to the standard formulation.
The intervention should be effective in systems in which phosphorus acts as a glass former.
Exceeding the phosphorus solubility limit may cause unwanted phase segregation.
Increasing phosphorus enhances local atomic-scale disorder.
Phosphorus-induced local disorder disrupts regular lattice formation and impedes long-range atomic ordering.
A modest phosphorus increase heightens atomic packing frustration.
Greater packing frustration impedes the diffusion and atomic rearrangements required for crystallization.
The phosphorus increase will lower the critical cooling rate required for glass formation.
The phosphorus increase will raise the crystallization onset temperature.
The benefit persists only while phosphorus remains soluble and homogeneously distributed.
Excessive phosphorus may produce phase segregation or brittle phosphide compounds that negate glass stabilization.
DSC, XRD, and TEM can be used to compare crystallization behavior and phase homogeneity between baseline and phosphorus-enhanced samples.

contradictions.description: The boundary treats phase segregation as a condition outside the intervention's expected range of benefit, whereas the falsification rule treats any observed phase segregation as falsifying the hypothesis. Without a quantified phosphorus increment or solubility boundary, these interpretations cannot be cleanly distinguished.
